content: 1. A study involving adults with heart failure demonstrated that the mean total all-cause costs per patient over an 18-month follow-up period were $4678 lower in the intervention group compared to the control group, with a confidence interval ranging from -4758 to -4597 USD. 2. Another study focusing on children with complex congenital heart disease found that delivering the intervention via videoconferencing was more cost-effective than standard care. 3. A study evaluating an e-health portal for children with a skin condition, which measured costs to both the healthcare system and parents, reported minimal or no differences in costs between the intervention and control groups. 4. Similarly, a study assessing the costs to the healthcare system of a PhysioDirect telephone intervention for musculoskeletal problems also reported little to no difference in costs compared to usual care. 5. The certainty of evidence regarding the effect of these interventions on healthcare costs was assessed as very low, making it difficult to draw definitive conclusions. 6. Studies conducted in hospital and primary care settings reported unintended consequences related to the interventions, but the evidence was inconsistent and of low certainty. 7. For adults with type 2 diabetes, major depression, heart conditions, dermatological issues, pulmonary diseases, musculoskeletal problems, and other conditions, as well as for older adults receiving home care, women post-delivery or post-abortion, and parents of children with asthma or food allergies, telemedicine interventions were compared to usual care. These interventions included phone-based consultations, home monitoring, web-delivered rehabilitation, and smartphone applications. 8. The settings for these studies varied, including community, primary care, and hospital-based environments in high-income countries (e.g., USA, UK, Germany) and middle-income countries (e.g., Turkey, Ecuador, Kenya). 9. The interventions were compared to usual care, which included standard medical management, face-to-face appointments, home visits, and referrals to specialists. Patients were also free to seek other treatments without specific recommendations. 10. Two studies reported minimal or no differences in adverse clinical events between intervention and control groups. 11. One study involving women who had undergone induced abortion found no significant differences in adverse effects, such as car accidents caused by mobile phone use while driving, between the intervention and control groups. 12. The certainty of evidence regarding the effect of interventions on healthcare costs for children and adults with heart-related conditions, as well as adults with musculoskeletal problems, was assessed as very low, limiting the reliability of conclusions. 13. The grading of evidence certainty (GRADE) ranged from high to very low, with many studies downgraded due to risks of bias, imprecision, inconsistency, and indirectness. 14. High-certainty evidence indicates confidence that the true effect is close to the estimated effect, while very low-certainty evidence suggests substantial uncertainty about the true effect. 15. Various tools and questionnaires, such as the Asthma Control Test (ACT), Diabetes Satisfaction and Treatment Questionnaire (DTSQ), and Pediatric Asthma Quality of Life Questionnaire (PACQLQ), were used to assess outcomes in these studies. 16. Many studies were downgraded due to unclear risks of bias, imprecision (e.g., wide confidence intervals), and limited generalizability to diverse settings or populations.
